title: Right livelihood

segments.voice: Yesterday: abhaya, freedom from fear, and the five precepts as great gifts. Your line: a gift to everyone.

Ask anyone at a party what they do, and they'll tell you their job. Not their hobbies, not their values: their job. Work fills a large share of a waking week. So it's striking that, of the eight factors on the Buddha's path, one is entirely about how you earn your living. Not whether you meditate on your lunch break. Not a prayer before the commute. The work itself, and what it does to people.
screen: `SO, WHAT DO YOU DO?` → `A LARGE SHARE OF THE WEEK.` → `ONE FACTOR FOR THE WORK ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Sammā ājīva. Ājīva means livelihood, the way a person keeps themselves alive, from jīva, life. In the great forty sutta, the definition is short: a noble disciple gives up wrong livelihood and makes a living by right livelihood. For the details, the canon looks in two directions. For monks and nuns, wrong livelihood has a surprising list. The first sutta of the Long Discourses names what it calls low arts: reading palms, interpreting dreams, predicting eclipses, picking lucky days, casting charms. The Buddha's monks weren't to live by any of them. And the great forty sutta names quieter wrongs: scheming, flattering, dropping hints for donations, belittling others to get gifts, and using one gift to fish for a bigger one. Fortune telling and sweet talk, it turns out, were how a holy person could make a living dishonestly. For lay people, the test is simpler: earn your living honestly, by your own effort, without harming. Tomorrow's sutta names specific trades to avoid. Right livelihood sits beside right speech and right action for a reason: it's speech and action done all day, every working day, for pay. A job can quietly ask you to shade the truth to a customer, cut a corner no one will see, or push people toward what they don't need. The path doesn't say quit your job. It says look at your work as honestly as you'd look at your words.
screen: `ĀJĪVA: HOW YOU KEEP ALIVE.` · `THE LOW ARTS: PALMS AND OMENS.` · `SCHEMING, HINTING, FLATTERING.` · `SPEECH AND ACTION, FOR PAY.` · then, large: `EARN CLEAN.`

segments.voice: Bring your work to mind, whatever it is, a job, caring for a family, studying, looking for work, and picture an ordinary hour of it. Ask first, without accusing yourself, where this work helps, and let that be clear. Then, gently, ask whether it anywhere asks you to shade the truth or harm someone a little, and just notice, with no verdicts today.
Sammā ājīva. Right livelihood: earning a living honestly and without harm. The fifth factor of the path.
Your line: earn clean. It's speech and action, done all day, for pay. That's day three hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Lay Buddhists reflect on whether their work causes harm, and some choose or change careers with right livelihood in mind; monastics live on what is freely offered and are not to earn by fortune telling or by flattering donors.
